source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can Large Language Models Explore In-Context?
finding: Across 3 LLMs and many prompt designs, almost no setup explores robustly in a bandit. Most fail by never pulling the best arm again after early rounds (suffix failure). A few fail by spreading pulls evenly (uniform failure).
numbers: Hard instance K=5 arms, gap 0.2, T=100, N=10 or 20 replicates per config. Gpt-4 basic prompt at T=500, N=20: over 60% of replicates show suffix failure, like Greedy. Gpt-4 table: SuffFailFreq(T/2) 0.50 for the basic prompt vs TS 0.01, UCB 0.02, Greedy 0.48.
quote: do not robustly engage in exploration without substantial interventions
limits: Small N and T; authors use surrogate statistics because reward alone is too noisy. Models are mid-2023 GPT-3.5, GPT-4-0613, Llama2-13B.
agent_relevance: A single-pass LLM allocator will lock onto an early leader. G12 needs an external rule for when to sample an option again.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can Large Language Models Explore In-Context?
finding: The one working setup was Gpt-4 with a hint to explore, per-arm summary statistics computed outside the model, and chain of thought. The same prompt with raw history failed.
numbers: 1 of the 72 Gpt-4 configurations (BSSC0) succeeded; no GPT-3.5 or Llama2 configuration did. Success matched Thompson Sampling reward at T=200, N=40.
limits: Summaries were per-arm averages, easy with 5 arms. With many arms or contexts each arm is played few times, so summaries help less (authors' own caveat).
agent_relevance: Compute the sufficient statistics (counts, means) in code and hand them to the model. Do not ask it to tally history itself.

source: Nie et al. (2024) EVOLvE: Evaluating and Optimizing LLMs For Exploration
finding: BanditBench shows LLMs fall well short of UCB in many bandits, and that putting UCB statistics into the prompt (algorithm-guided support) or fine-tuning on UCB traces closes much of the gap for larger models.
numbers: Overall win-rate, multi-armed bandit, raw history vs algorithm-guided: Gemma-2B 7.6 vs 4.9, Gemma-9B 10.5 vs 4.1, Gemini-1.5 Flash 27.7 vs 32.2, Pro 45.5 vs 59.6. Contextual bandit: Flash 0.0 vs 46.4, Pro 7.1 vs 64.3. UCB itself: 90.6 (MAB), 96.4 (CB). 30 runs per setup, t-test p<0.05; 16 MAB configs, horizons 200 and 1000.
limits: Small models (Gemma 2B/9B) got worse with algorithm guidance. Stateless bandits only.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that a scaffold which computes the index outside the model beats the model's own judgment, but only for models big enough to use it.

source: Nie et al. (2024) EVOLvE
finding: Distilling UCB behaviour: few-shot demonstrations and fine-tuning react in opposite ways to the data format and to demonstration difficulty. Few-shot even hurt the bigger model.
numbers: Few-shot with summarised history: 50.2% win-rate vs 27.5% with raw history. Fine-tuning shows the reverse: raw history 65.6 vs summarised 28.3. Few-shot trained on easy tasks 50.2 vs hard 43.0; fine-tuning on hard 65.6 vs easy 54.5. Few-shot hurt Gemini-1.5 Pro in MAB and CB.
limits: Authors hypothesise that hand-written few-shot examples disrupt chain of thought in larger models; not tested.
agent_relevance: Examples in the prompt can backfire; test any prompt-side allocation rule against a no-example control.

source: Nie et al. (2024) EVOLvE
finding: Regret curves were fit with a log-versus-linear parametric form: guided or fine-tuned models show sublinear regret, weak ones stay near linear.
numbers: Gemma 2B and 9B remain in the linear-regret regime; Flash with algorithm-guided support or fine-tuning reaches near sublinear regret.
limits: Fit over short horizons; sublinear versus linear is hard to tell at T=200.
agent_relevance: Use a regret-trend check, not final reward, to judge whether an allocator really learns.

source: Park et al. (2024) Do LLM Agents Have Regret? A Case Study in Online Learning and Games
finding: In adversarial online learning, pre-trained LLMs often reach sublinear regret, sometimes below FTRL in games. But GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo failed on simple crafted loss sequences.
numbers: Failing cases: noisy alternating loss and an adaptive loss (adversary puts loss 10 on the arm GPT-4 favours). Over 20 repeats the hypothesis of linear regret could not be rejected for GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo.
limits: Adversarial (non-stochastic) setting with small action sets, not the stochastic bandit behind Gittins.
agent_relevance: An agent that trusts its own recent pattern can be fooled by structured payoffs; the allocator needs a guard against its own streak.

source: Park et al. (2024) Do LLM Agents Have Regret?
finding: Partial check of the Krishnamurthy claim that summarised history is the key. In the online-learning setting the raw versus summarised input changed regret significantly, so the effect depends on the setting.
numbers: Regret differed between the two input types with p = 1.2e-157 (one-sided independent t-test); the authors say the settings differ fundamentally from Krishnamurthy et al.
limits: Different loss structure, not a direct re-run of the stochastic bandit.
agent_relevance: Do not assume one input format is best for all allocation tasks; test both.

source: Monea et al. (2025) LLMs Are In-Context Bandit Reinforcement Learners
finding: Contextual-bandit in-context RL works, but only if exploration is forced. Naive prompting stalls; keeping only positive-reward episodes and randomly sampling which episodes enter the prompt (Stochastic ICRL) fixes it.
numbers: Banking77 (77 labels): Qwen2.5-7B from 6.2% zero-shot to 72.2% with Stochastic ICRL, no gold labels, no weight updates. Qwen models 0.5B to 72B: bigger is better at every size. Stochastic ICRL held up when 10% of rewards were inverted.
limits: Learning from negative rewards is poor: models struggle to reason about their own errors. Naive ICRL is less stable.
agent_relevance: Exploration can be injected by randomising which past attempts the model sees. Keep successes; do not feed failures back as signals.

source: Schmied et al. (2025) LLMs are Greedy Agents: Effects of RL Fine-tuning on Decision-Making Abilities
finding: Three failure modes in bandits: greediness (stop trying new arms), frequency bias (copy the most common action in context), and a knowing-doing gap.
numbers: Gemma2, 64 bandits, 10 arms, 50 steps: 2B covers 40% of arms, 9B and 27B cover 65%; without chain of thought only 25%. With 20 arms the largest cover 45%. Models give correct rationales 87% of the time yet pick the greedy action in 64% of those cases.
limits: Gemma2 only, 50 interaction steps, synthetic Gaussian bandits.
agent_relevance: More thinking does not cure greediness; reasoning text can be right and the action still wrong (supports G10).

source: Schmied et al. (2025) LLMs are Greedy Agents
finding: RL fine-tuning on the model's own chain of thought lowers regret, but exploration stays below UCB. A simple bonus fixes much of it.
numbers: Exploration bonus (+1 reward for an untried action during RL fine-tuning): action coverage 50% to 70% and lower regret. Fine-tuned 2B narrows the gap to larger models and UCB. Chain of thought is called a vital exploration mechanism.
limits: Needs training, so not a scaffold-only result. At 20 arms the 9B and 27B beat UCB only because of the short 50-step horizon (authors' note).
agent_relevance: A scaffold analogue of the bonus is a forced try of every option before any commitment.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 did well in a bandit and the horizon task, but showed random exploration only in part and no directed exploration.
numbers: Whole horizon-task experiment: GPT-3 mean regret 2.72 (SD 5.98) vs humans 3.24 (SD 10.26), t(38878) = -5.03, p<.001. Short horizon: indistinguishable from humans, p=.97. Long horizon: humans improved more within a game. No horizon-by-reward-difference interaction and no positive horizon effect in the unequal-information condition. It preferred the option it had seen more often.
limits: text-davinci-002 era model; 4 forced plus 1 or 6 free trials; newer models not tested here.
agent_relevance: A model can look good on regret and still not value information about under-sampled options, the thing the Gittins index prizes.

source: Coda-Forno et al. (2023) Meta-in-context learning in large language models
finding: Showing GPT-3 a series of bandit tasks in one prompt improves later tasks: it adapts its priors, not its weights.
numbers: Two-armed bandit, 500 simulations, 10 trials per task, means from N(0,64), noise N(0,32): after 4 earlier tasks GPT-3 matched a greedy policy and trailed UCB slightly. In-context learning coefficient on regret beta = -0.221 +/- 0.012 (t = -35.8).
limits: Only text-davinci-002 and two arms; matching greedy is a low bar since greedy is known to fail on hard instances (Krishnamurthy).
agent_relevance: Carrying a ledger of earlier similar problems into the prompt can improve allocation.

source: Schubert et al. (2024) In-context learning agents are asymmetric belief updaters
finding: In a two-armed bandit, LLMs learn more from better-than-expected outcomes (optimism). The bias flips for the unchosen option and vanishes when told someone else is sampling.
numbers: Four casinos, win probabilities 0.25/0.25, 0.25/0.75, 0.75/0.25, 0.75/0.75; 24 visits each. LLM improvement was similar to the human data of Lefebvre et al. 2017. Rescorla-Wagner fits showed a higher learning rate for positive errors on chosen options.
limits: Framing of agency changes the bias, so results depend on prompt wording. Model-family details not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Optimism after wins inflates the value of the current leader; phrase the allocator as a neutral observer.

source: Auer, Cesa-Bianchi and Fischer (2002) Finite-time Analysis of the Multiarmed Bandit Problem
finding: UCB1 achieves logarithmic regret uniformly over time with no knowledge of the reward distributions, using a bonus sqrt(2 ln n / n_j).
numbers: The bound has a term 8 ln n / delta_i^2 per suboptimal arm. On 7 Bernoulli distributions (figures 6 to 12), UCB1-Tuned was substantially better than UCB1 (no proof for Tuned). A well-tuned epsilon_n-greedy usually did best; mis-tuned it degraded rapidly and lost when many arms were clearly bad.
limits: Experiments only Bernoulli rewards; epsilon_n-greedy needs the gap to be tuned.
agent_relevance: Confidence-bound allocation is cheap and tuning-light; a fixed epsilon is not.

source: Agrawal and Goyal (2012) Analysis of Thompson Sampling for the multi-armed bandit problem
finding: First proof that Thompson Sampling (a 1933 idea) gets logarithmic expected regret in stochastic bandits.
numbers: Two arms: O(ln T / delta + 1/delta^3). N arms: O((sum 1/delta_i^2)^2 ln T). Bounds are optimal but for small factors.
limits: Beta-Bernoulli proofs; the empirical edge over UCB comes from other studies not read here.
agent_relevance: Sample-from-belief is a principled, simple rule an LLM can imitate by drawing from its own stated uncertainty.

source: Russo, Van Roy, Kazerouni, Osband and Wen (2018) A Tutorial on Thompson Sampling
finding: Explains why greedy fails (never retries an arm wrongly rated low), why epsilon-greedy wastes trials on arms that are clearly bad, and why sampling from the posterior writes off bad arms.
numbers: Worked beta-Bernoulli three-armed example comparing the probability that greedy and TS select each arm.
limits: Review with illustrative examples, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Clearest statement of why uniform and greedy allocation both lose.

source: Bubeck, Munos and Stoltz (2011) Pure Exploration in Finitely-Armed and Continuous-Armed Bandits
finding: If the goal is the final recommendation, not reward during the test phase, the best strategy changes: lower cumulative regret in exploration forces higher simple regret.
numbers: Theorem 1 gives a lower bound on simple regret in terms of cumulative regret. Uniform exploration is a good benchmark when the number of exploration rounds is large.
limits: Asymptotic bounds.
agent_relevance: Our agent often pays for attempts first and picks one answer later. That is pure exploration, so UCB-style exploitation of the leader is the wrong objective.

source: Li, Jamieson, DeSalvo, Rostamizadeh and Talwalkar (2018) Hyperband
finding: Bandit allocation by successive halving across brackets, trading the number of configurations against resources each, beats Bayesian-optimisation baselines.
numbers: Reports over an order-of-magnitude speedup over competitors (SMAC, TPE, Spearmint) on deep-learning and kernel problems; overhead under 5% on EC2.
limits: Assumes early loss predicts final loss; the paper names an 'n versus B/n' problem for naive halving.
agent_relevance: Successive halving is a practical budget rule for many candidate attempts: cut weak ones early, spend on survivors.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Coverage (fraction solved by any of k samples) grows log-linearly over orders of magnitude of k, so extra spend pays when a verifier exists; selection without a verifier plateaus.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: DeepSeek-Coder-V2 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250, beating the 43% single-sample state of the art. CodeContests, Gemma-2B: 0.02% to 7.1% with 10,000 samples (over 300x). MATH, Llama-3-8B: coverage 82.9% at 1 sample, rising with k.
limits: Majority voting and reward models plateau beyond several hundred samples; gains need an automatic checker.
agent_relevance: With a checker, more samples nearly always pay on solvable problems; without one the spend is wasted, which supports G12.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu and Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: The best way to spend test-time compute depends on question difficulty. A per-prompt compute-optimal policy beats best-of-N.
numbers: More than 4x efficiency over best-of-N (about 4x less compute) with revisions and with PRM search. FLOPs-matched, a smaller model with test-time compute beats a 14x larger model on easy and intermediate questions.
quote: where a smaller base model attains somewhat non-trivial success rates
limits: On the hardest questions test-time compute gives very little benefit; the 14x result holds only where the small model has non-trivial success. PaLM 2-S* on MATH.
agent_relevance: Direct support for spend by difficulty and search only with a foothold (G12).

source: Damani et al. (2024) Learning How Hard to Think: Input-Adaptive Allocation of LM Computation
finding: Predict each query's reward-versus-budget curve and allocate samples where the marginal gain is highest; also route queries between a cheap and an expensive decoder.
numbers: Up to 50% less computation at no quality loss, or up to 10% better quality at fixed budget (code and math). Chat: matches reward with up to 10% less compute. Many Code problems have 0% success and can be answered 'I don't know' to free their samples. Offline variant always beat best-of-k; online variant fell below best-of-k at high budgets.
limits: Needs a learned difficulty predictor and training data; online variant failed at high budgets.
agent_relevance: Allocate by predicted marginal gain and skip hopeless items. A zero-success flag is a stop signal.

source: Zuo and Zhu (2026) Strategic Scaling of Test-Time Compute: A Bandit Learning Approach
finding: Treat each query as an arm; learn difficulty on the fly and prefer solvable hard queries. Provably needs less budget than uniform allocation.
numbers: Up to 11.10% absolute (15.04% relative) on MATH-500, 10.82% (14.44%) on AIME25, 11.23% (15.29%) on LiveCodeBench. At average budget 16 Llama-3.2-1B accuracy +2.50% (1.82x efficiency), Llama-3.1-8B +1.40% (2x); coverage +11.10% at budget 8 (3.93x). Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite +3.4% accuracy, over 2x efficiency. Theory: uniform needs the max over queries of 1/gap^2, adaptive needs a sum.
limits: Needs a reward oracle (PRM, ground truth or LLM judge). The explore-then-commit baseline was clearly beaten. Accuracy gain on a strong model is small (3.4%).
agent_relevance: Closest published match to an in-agent bandit allocator over problems; sets expected size of the win.

source: Manvi, Singh and Ermon (2024) Adaptive Inference-Time Compute: LLMs Can Predict if They Can Do Better, Even Mid-Generation
finding: The model can predict mid-generation whether restarting would give a better answer, which supports stopping or pruning samples.
numbers: Llama 3.1 8B win rate vs GPT-4 on AlpacaEval 21% to 34% with 16 samples; GSM8K 84% to 91%. 74% of the 16-sample gain with 1.2 samples on average; 50 to 75% of samples pruned early with minimal loss.
limits: Needs a trained self-evaluation head on LMSYS prompts; not a prompt-only result.
agent_relevance: A cheap self-estimate of 'would another try help' is workable as a stop rule.

source: Gershman (2018) Deconstructing the human algorithms for exploration
finding: Two experiments separate UCB-like uncertainty bonuses (bias shift) from Thompson-like sampling (slope shift). Humans show both; a hybrid model fits best.
numbers: Exp 1 N=44, Exp 2 N=45 (Mechanical Turk). First-trial preference for the uncertain arm in Exp 1: t(44)=9.68, p<0.001; none in Exp 2 (p=0.95). Total uncertainty slowed responses (t(44)=12.64); relative uncertainty sped them only in Exp 2 (t(43)=2.39).
limits: Online samples; Gaussian rewards; the knowledge-gradient form of directed exploration (Zhang and Yu 2013) is not ruled out.
agent_relevance: Humans use a bonus and sampling together; a hybrid allocator (count bonus plus sampled belief) is a defensible target.

source: Gershman (2018) re-analysis of Wilson et al. (2014) horizon-task data
finding: Re-analysis of the Wilson et al. 2014 data (directed plus random exploration): choices were decisively better explained by the hybrid model than by pure UCB or pure Thompson.
numbers: Wilson task: two options, means 40 or 60, SD 8, blocks of 5 to 10 trials; hybrid protected exceedance probability 0.999.
limits: Second-hand: Wilson 2014 itself was not opened; this reports only what Gershman wrote.
agent_relevance: Sets the human benchmark that the LLM studies (Binz and Schulz) are compared against.

source: Healthy cognitive aging and directed and random exploration in the Horizon Task (2024), authors not recorded
finding: Moderator is age. Older adults explore with both strategies but less than younger adults. About a quarter avoid information entirely and do worse.
numbers: 51 older adults (65 to 74) and 32 younger adults (18 to 25). About 26% of older adults had information seeking near zero and lower task scores.
limits: Authors not recorded; small samples; one task.
agent_relevance: Individual differences in information avoidance matter; the agent needs a guard against skipping informative options.

source: Phelps et al. (2025) The dynamics of explore-exploit decisions suggest a threshold mechanism for reduced random exploration in older adults
finding: A drift diffusion model of the horizon task: older adults have lower signal-to-noise and a higher decision threshold. The threshold explains the reduced random exploration.
numbers: Fit to choices and response times in younger and older adults (sample sizes not recorded from my read of the abstract).
limits: Model-based inference; threshold and signal-to-noise can trade off.
agent_relevance: Little direct bearing on an LLM; useful only as a moderator in the human record.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Gittins index
finding: Gittins index policy is optimal for independent arms, discounted reward, and only the played arm changing. Many algorithms compute the index.
numbers: Gittins and collaborators in the 1970s; Whittle (1980) retirement-process view; Weitzman reached the same result in economics. Computation: Varaiya, Chen-Katehakis (LP), Katehakis-Veinott restart-in-state, Sonin elimination (2004), Nino-Mora (2007).
limits: Secondary source; the 1979 paper was not opened. The conditions rarely hold for LLM attempts, which are correlated, not independent.
agent_relevance: If attempts are correlated, the optimality guarantee does not apply; use the index as a guide, not a proof.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Gittins index, restless bandits
finding: If several projects can change at once (restless bandits), the Gittins policy is only a heuristic and no exact feasible solution is known in general.
numbers: Article says it is generally accepted that no feasible solution can be found.
limits: Same secondary source.
agent_relevance: Our problems drift while we wait, so restless-bandit logic applies and Gittins is only approximate.
